------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#reproducibility-explained data-menu-title="Reproducibility Explained"}

[Reproducibility as Scientific Integrity]{.slide-title}

![Artwork by Allison
Horst](../../images/r_provenance_reproducibility/reproducibility_alibi_horst.png){width="55%"
fig-align="center"}

::: body-text
**Without reproducibility:**

\- Can't verify results

\- Can't build on prior work

\- Can't trust conclusions

**Reproducibility isn't optional—it's essential**

**It's your scientific alibi**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#definition data-menu-title="Definition"}

[What Is Reproducibility?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Reproducibility** = Someone else can take your data and code and get
the same results

**Not:** - Replicability (collecting new data) - Just having data
available - Describing methods in prose

**Is:** - Exact same results from same inputs - Including all
intermediate steps - With clear documentation
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#crisis data-menu-title="Reproducibility Crisis"}

[The Reproducibility Crisis]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Studies show:**

\- 70% of researchers have tried and failed to reproduce another's work

\- 50% have failed to reproduce their OWN work

\- Less than 30% of published studies share data AND code

**In biology/ecology:**

\- Many analyses impossible to reproduce

\- Methods sections insufficient

\- Code rarely shared
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#why-fails-intro data-menu-title="Why Fails Introduction"}

[Why Does Reproducibility Fail?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Not because scientists are careless!**

Reproducibility fails due to:

1\. Undocumented decisions

2\. Fragile computational environments

3\. Manual steps

4\. Ambiguous workflows

5\. Time pressure

**Let's examine each...**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#undocumented-decisions data-menu-title="Undocumented Decisions"}

[Reason 1: Undocumented Decisions]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**The problem:**

You try outlier removal thresholds: 2 SD, 2.5 SD, 3 SD

You pick 2.5 SD (seems reasonable)

**You don't write this down**

Six months later: Which threshold did you use?

**Methods say:** "Outliers were removed"

**Reviewer asks:** "How were outliers defined?"

**You:** ¯\_(ツ)\_/¯
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#fragile-environments data-menu-title="Fragile Environments"}

[Reason 2: Fragile Computational Environments]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**The problem:**

Your analysis runs on: - R version 4.2.1 - ggplot2 version 3.4.0 - Your
computer

**Collaborator has:** - R version 4.3.0 - ggplot2 version 3.4.2 -
Different computer

**Result:** Different results or errors

**Why?** Package versions matter, OS matters
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#manual-steps data-menu-title="Manual Steps"}

[Reason 3: Manual Steps]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**The problem:**

Your workflow: 1. Export data from instrument 2. Open in Excel, delete
bad rows 3. Save as CSV 4. Run R script 5. Open plot, adjust colors in
Photoshop 6. Insert in manuscript

**Which rows deleted? What colors? Can't reconstruct!**

**Solution:** Everything in code
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#solution-intro data-menu-title="Solution Introduction"}

[The Solution: Reproducible Workflows]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Core principle:**

**Everything in code + version control**

This solves:

\- ✅ Undocumented decisions → Comments in code

\- ✅ Fragile environments → Document packages

\- ✅ Manual steps → Automate in code

\- ✅ Ambiguous workflows → Clear structure

\- ✅ Time pressure → Build habits now
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#checklist data-menu-title="Reproducibility Checklist"}

[Reproducibility Checklist]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Before sharing/publishing:**

-   [ ] All steps in code (no manual steps)
-   [ ] Decisions documented in comments
-   [ ] File paths are relative
-   [ ] README explains how to run
-   [ ] Package versions documented
-   [ ] Code runs start-to-finish without errors
-   [ ] Someone else has successfully run it

**If you can't check all boxes, it's not reproducible**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#breakout data-menu-title="Breakout Activity"}

[Breakout Activity - 12 minutes]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Scenario:** Student's analysis can't be reproduced

**Files:**

\- `data_final.csv`

\- `analysis_old.R`

\- `analysis_NEW.R`

\- Several plots

\- Methods: "Data were cleaned and outliers removed"

**In groups:** 1. List everything that's missing for reproducibility 2.
Redesign the workflow to be reproducible 3. What specific documentation
is needed?
:::

[Before Wednesday]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Reading:** Git/GitHub introduction (on Canvas)

**Task:** Review YOUR current project

**Ask yourself:**

1\. Could someone else reproduce my analysis?

2\. What manual steps do I have?

3\. What decisions are undocumented?

4\. Is my workflow clear?

**Be honest:** Identifying problems is the first step
:::

##  {#summary data-menu-title="Summary"}

[Key Concepts]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
1.  **Reproducibility** = same data + code → same results

2.  **Most research isn't reproducible** (and that's a problem)

3.  **Five reasons:** Undocumented decisions, fragile environments,
    manual steps, ambiguous workflows, time pressure

4.  **Solution:** Everything in code + version control

5.  **Wednesday:** Git/GitHub as reproducibility infrastructure

**See you Wednesday!**
:::
